The Story of the Observance of Humility

I bow to Lord Jina, worshipped by Indra, Dharanendra, Chakravartins, and other great beings, and I write the sacred story of those who observe the dharma of humility.

In the land of Vats, in the famous city of Kaushambi, King Dhanasen was a follower of Vaishnav dharma. His queen Dhanashri, who was very beautiful and learned, practised Jain dharma. She had taken the vows of a layman. In that city lived a Vaishnav ascetic named Supratishth. The king honoured him greatly and personally seated him on a high seat to feed him. This ascetic possessed a knowledge called Jalstambhini, by which he would stand in the middle of the Yamuna River and worship God without drowning. Seeing such power, foolish people were greatly amazed. Truly, fools always admire foolish displays.

In Rathnupur, south of Vijayardh Mountain, King Vidyutprabh was a Jain who observed the vows of a layman, while his queen Vidyudvega was a follower of Vaishnav dharma. One day, while enjoying the beauty of nature, the royal couple came to Kaushambi. Reaching the riverbank, they saw an ascetic standing in the middle of the Yamuna, practising austerity. Vidyutprabh knew that this was a false-faith ascetic. But his queen Vidyudvega praised the ascetic greatly.

Vidyutprabh said to his queen, "Very well, my dear, come — let me show you this person's foolishness." Then both of them disguised themselves as Chandalas and went upstream, where they began washing the hides of dead animals in the river. Through this despicable act, they polluted the water. The ascetic was greatly disturbed by this. He scolded them and moved upstream. There he bathed and washed again. Truly, people do all manner of things under the influence of foolishness.

Seeing the ascetic's foolishness, the king and queen went even further upstream and began washing hides again. The ascetic, seeing their repeated mischief, became very angry. He moved further away. But they followed him and continued their prank. In short, they gave the ascetic great trouble. At last, the poor ascetic had to abandon his meditation and worship entirely.

Afterward, through the power of their knowledge, the king and queen built a great palace in the forest for the ascetic, showing him that true spiritual power lies not in dramatic displays but in the practice of non-violence, compassion, and humility. The ascetic, humbled by this experience, began to question the validity of his own practices. Eventually, through the grace of Jain dharma, he came to understand the true path and took right faith.

This story teaches that humility is a essential virtue on the spiritual path. Those who display their spiritual powers for the sake of admiration are like the Vaishnav ascetic — easily disturbed and ultimately misguided. The wise should practise humility and non-violence, for these are the true marks of spiritual advancement.
